claims.text: High configurational entropy combined with significant lattice distortion creates sluggish diffusion kinetics in near-equiatomic high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses phase separation and chemical segregation at elevated service temperatures.
Suppression of phase separation preserves the single-phase structure needed for stable catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
The relevant initial materials are homogeneous, single-phase, near-equiatomic nanoparticles with random elemental arrangements.
Pre-annealing at approximately 700 K in an inert atmosphere modifies diffusion kinetics before service exposure.
Catalytic service occurs over 773–1173 K and thermoelectric service over 473–1923 K.
Atomic-size differences produce lattice distortion in a high-configurational-entropy matrix.
Lattice distortion acts as an energy barrier to atomic mobility.
High configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes a single-phase solid solution.
High diffusion barriers prevent phase separation and elemental segregation even after prolonged elevated-temperature exposure.
A near-equiatomic Nb-Ta-Ti-V alloy can remain a single BCC solid solution up to 900 °C.
Preventing segregation maintains the active, compositionally uniform surface required for catalytic and thermoelectric functionality.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles will undergo less phase and chemical change during high-temperature exposure than otherwise identical as-synthesized controls.
As-synthesized controls may develop phase segregation or elemental redistribution during prolonged elevated-temperature exposure.
The proposed stabilization may fail in alloys with strong element-specific segregation tendencies or in oxidizing environments dominated by surface reactions.
Diffusion activation energies and long-term stability thresholds for the nanoparticles remain quantitatively uncertain.
